cards.text: The Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), has been looking hard at life under the sun. Now he tells a little story he calls great wisdom. There was a small city with only a few men in it.

cards.question: Trouble is coming for that small city with only a few men. Who comes against it?

cards.text: A mighty king surrounds the city and builds large siege ramps against it. Friend, that's like showing up to a cookie bake-off with one spatula while the other guy rolls in with a WHOLE FACTORY.

cards.question: The small city is surrounded and the siege ramps are going up. Who saves the city?
After the poor wise man saves the city by his wisdom, everyone remembers him.
The Teacher says wisdom is better than strength. But what happens to the poor man's wisdom?

answers.text: People despise it and ignore his words
Kings write it down to use later
The city pays him gold to hear it

cards.text: Then the Teacher puts two voices side by side: the calm words of the wise, and the shouts of a ruler among fools. Quiet versus LOUD, baker, and only one of them gets heeded.

cards.question: The Teacher says the shouts of a ruler among fools are heeded over the calm words of the wise.

cards.text: Next the Teacher says wisdom is better than weapons of war. Then he warns how much damage sin can do.

cards.question: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one ___ destroys much good.

cards.text: Now a picture: somebody's fancy perfumer's oil gets a few dead flies in it, and the whole thing stinks. EXPENSIVE stink, friend.

cards.question: What is the Teacher's point with the dead flies in the perfumer's oil?

answers.text: A little folly outweighs wisdom and honor
Perfume should always be kept covered
Wise men should stay far from flies

cards.text: A wise man's heart inclines to the right, but a fool's heart inclines to the left. Then the fool heads out for a walk down the road.

cards.question: As the fool walks along the road, he manages to keep his folly hidden from everyone.

cards.text: Next the Teacher says what to do if the ruler's temper flares against you. Friend, every part of me would be backing slowly toward the door, gold base and all.

cards.question: If the ruler's temper flares against you, do not abandon your ___, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.

cards.text: Then the Teacher names an error that comes from the ruler: folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions. Mr. Reply-All just got promoted to CEO.

cards.question: The Teacher describes a world flipped upside down. What has he seen?

answers.text: Slaves on horseback and princes on foot
Priests in fields and farmers in temples
Soldiers at feasts and kings at the gate

cards.text: Then the Teacher looks at a couple of jobs: he who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake. And I thought MY biggest work hazard was a hot oven.

cards.question: The Teacher says the one who splits logs is perfectly safe.

cards.text: If the axe is dull, you have to put more strength into every swing. Baker, I KNOW dull: my edges got so soft that Mother Miller had to press a little harder, and she smiled a little less at every cookie.

cards.question: A dull axe takes more strength. So what does the Teacher say produces success?
A snake charmer still profits if the snake bites before it is charmed.

cards.text: Now the Teacher talks about talking. The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious.

cards.question: A wise man's words are gracious, but the lips of a fool ___ him.
The Teacher follows a fool's talk from beginning to end. How does it go?

answers.text: Starts foolish and ends even worse
Starts foolish and ends up wise
Starts wise and ends up foolish

cards.text: Yet the fool multiplies words. He's the guy who sends forty-seven texts to the group chat to say ONE thing, and then a voice memo to explain the texts.

cards.question: The fool multiplies words, but the Teacher says no one knows what is coming. So someone can surely tell him what will come after him.

cards.text: Then the fool goes to work, and his toil just wears him OUT.

cards.question: Why does the fool's toil wear him out?

answers.text: He does not know the way to the city
He carries heavy stones for the king
He works all night without any rest

cards.text: Then the Teacher turns to whole lands. Woe to the land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning.

cards.question: Blessed is the land whose king is a son of nobles and whose princes feast at the proper time. What do those princes feast for?

answers.text: For strength and not for drunkenness
For praise and not for peace
For show and not for hunger

cards.text: Now the Teacher looks at a roof caving in and a house that leaks.

cards.question: Through ___ the roof caves in, and in the hands of the ___ the house leaks.

cards.text: That's the drip in the ceiling you promised to fix next weekend, three years ago. Then the Teacher says a feast is prepared for laughter and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.
Last word from the Teacher: do not curse the king, even in your thoughts. And do not curse the rich, even in your bedroom.

cards.question: The Teacher says not to curse the king or the rich, even in private. Why not?

answers.text: A bird of the air may carry your words
The palace walls hear every word
The king can read every heart

findings.problem: The card calls 9:13-15 'a little story he calls great wisdom.' The text doesn't call it a story. It is 'this wisdom' the Teacher has 'seen under the sun,' and he says 'it was great to me.' Calling it a story he tells could make it sound like a made-up parable instead of something he saw.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The right answer 'A mighty king' is one generic person. Both wrong answers are named groups ('A Philistine army', 'A band of Amalekites'). Because it is a different kind of answer, the right one stands out as the odd one.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This is a 'who' question, but the wrong answers 'A rich young soldier' and 'A famous old general' are made up. They are not real details from anywhere in the Bible.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: 'Only one of them gets heeded' stretches 9:17. The verse says the calm words of the wise 'are heeded over' the shouts, which is a comparison. It does not say the shouts get no hearing at all. The line is a claim about the text, not part of a joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The setup says the Teacher 'warns how much damage sin can do.' That gives away the blank on card 10 ('one ___ destroys much good'): with 'sin' just mentioned, 'sinner' is obvious over 'soldier' and 'stranger'.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'Perfume should always be kept covered' and 'Wise men should stay far from flies' are literal and close to silly. Next to them, the right answer, which is the verse's own wording, clearly stands out as the Bible-sounding one.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess a word of the BSB line ('post' vs 'city' vs 'friends'). The meaning, which is to stay put and stay calm, fits more than one choice. Only knowing the wording picks 'post'.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The joke names Mother Miller without saying who she is. The docs say bakers know about the junk drawer from onboarding, and that the kids' names are highlighted with a tap-to-see pop-up. The docs don't say whether bakers know Mother Miller, or that his edges wore down before the drawer. The line is also more wistful than funny.
findings.question: Do bakers meet Mother Miller and the worn-down-edges part of the backstory in onboarding, so Papa Dorin can name her without introducing her? If not, does he need to say who she is, like 'the lady who owned me'?

findings.problem: The true-or-false statement includes its own answer: it says 'no one knows what is coming' and then claims 'So someone can surely tell him.' That rules out True. It also adds a 'but' and a 'So' that join the clauses of 10:14 in ways the text doesn't.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'Now the Teacher looks at a roof caving in and a house that leaks.' This is a bare summary with none of Papa Dorin's voice. Several other stop 2 story cards (6, 13, 18) are almost as plain.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: 'That's the drip in the ceiling you promised to fix next weekend, three years ago' makes the baker the lazy one the joke laughs at. The laziness joke should land on Papa Dorin himself.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'The palace walls hear every word' is the 'walls have ears' idea. It means close to the same thing as the right answer: your private words will get out and be reported. A baker could argue it's right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.
